title: Who are the Amish?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain who the Amish are: origins in 1693-era Swiss Mennonite split led by Jacob Ammann, settlement in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania (1770s arrival), rejection of violence and military service, plain dress, shunning of electricity and vanity, Ordnung community rules, rumspringa and baptism at about sixteen, shunning of those who leave permanently, courtship via singing and front-porch visits, November weddings announced by the deacon, faceless dolls, quilts, farming and craft trade through Mennonite middlemen, dairy farms with modern equipment and FDA standards, schooling to eighth grade, not paying Social Security, and how the Amish adopt technology selectively. Closes with listener mail about an Amazon tribe contact story and a courtship story.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with casual banter, then introduce the topic of the Amish and their arrival in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania.

segments.title: Origins and the Amish split from the Mennonites
segments.summary: The Amish are described as a Christian sect formed in the 1600s by Swiss Mennonite Jacob Ammann, who opposed foot washing twice-yearly communion and mingling with society. The Amish are located in Lancaster County, Ohio, Indiana, Utah and Canada.

segments.title: Plain dress, hats, and beards
segments.summary: Men wear dark suits, blue shirts, suspenders and black brimmed hats, with hat shape varying; women wear frock dresses, black capes and bonnets after baptism. Married men wear short beards without mustaches, which are associated with the military.

segments.title: Pacifism and conscientious objection
segments.summary: The Amish reject violence, including self-defense, and have historically been conscripted into non-combat roles. Some conscientious objectors during World War Two were placed in state mental hospitals and helped expose conditions there.

segments.title: Baptism, rumspringa, and shunning
segments.summary: Amish practice believer baptism around age sixteen, unlike infant baptism. Young people may spend about a year in rumspringa living among the English, sometimes involving drugs such as crystal meth and the documentary The Double's Playground. Those who leave after baptism are shunned permanently; those who leave before baptism can return.

segments.title: Courtship, weddings and the deacon's announcement
segments.summary: Courtship happens through singing services and front-porch visits with chaperones. Men give practical gifts such as butter churns. Weddings occur in November, announced by the deacon two weeks after fall communion, and held at the bride's home, with the couple living with the bride's parents afterward.

segments.title: Farming, quilts, dolls, and community life
segments.summary: The Amish grow corn, wheat, tobacco, soybeans, barley and potatoes, and make furniture and sheds. Amish quilts rose to thousands of dollars in the 1980s. Amish dolls have no faces. Barn raising and the community pot help young couples buy farms; Amish live without a credit or cash emphasis and earn wealth mainly through land.

segments.title: Technology, dairy farms, trade, and government relations
segments.summary: The Amish selectively adopt technology that does not undermine community, using gas or diesel power off the grid. Dairy farms use electric milking equipment to meet FDA standards. They sell through Mennonite middlemen, pay property taxes but not Social Security, and schooling is compulsory through eighth grade. Amish may travel by plane without owning or operating vehicles.

segments.title: Joining the Amish, funerals, and health care
segments.summary: Outsiders can join but it is rare, requiring fluency in Low German. The Amish do not proselytize. Funerals are plain with no flowers, and Amish use embalmers and medical care. Amish use hazard triangles and flashers on buggies. Practices vary locally under the Ordnung. Chuck's twist about the Lancaster focus is noted.

segments.title: Listener mail: Amazon tribe contact and courtship stories
segments.summary: A listener's father-in-law recounts a primitive tribe contact in the Amazon rainforest in the early eighties, including an arrow attack. Josh and Chuck also invite listeners to send romantic courtship stories for Valentine's Day.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close with website information and an ad read.
